opus-5.5.text:
I think the outside view people are drawing on is actually pretty reasonable on its face, so it's worth steelmanning it before I say where I part ways with it.

The basic picture goes something like this: for roughly the last 150 years, frontier economies like the US have grown at about two percent per year per capita, remarkably steadily. In that time we've had electricity, the internal combustion engine, antibiotics, the telephone, computers, the internet, smartphones. Each of these felt revolutionary to the people living through it, and each one did transform daily life. But when you look at the aggregate growth numbers, you don't see big spikes. The trend line just keeps chugging along. So someone with that history in mind looks at AI and says: this is another general-purpose technology, probably a very important one, but the base rate says important technologies get absorbed into the economy at a pace that keeps us near that two percent line. Maybe it bumps us up to two and a half or three percent for a while. That's the outside view.

Underneath that there are some more specific mechanisms people point to. One is diffusion lag. It took decades for factories to reorganize around electric motors rather than just swapping them in for steam engines, and the productivity gains only showed up once the whole workflow was redesigned. Another is bottlenecks, a sort of Baumol's cost disease argument: even if AI makes some tasks nearly free, the economy ends up constrained by whatever remains slow and human, whether that's physical construction, regulatory approval, clinical trials, or just people needing to trust and adopt new things. Growth gets limited by the slowest essential input. And then there's institutional and social friction. Licensing, liability, incumbents protecting their turf, and people simply not wanting to change how they work.

Where I think that view runs into trouble is that it treats AI as one more entry in the list of technologies, when the thing that has stayed constant across that whole 150-year period is that humans were doing the inventing, the deploying, and the reorganizing. Population and the number of researchers were the engine behind the steady trend. If you get AI systems that can substitute for human cognitive labor broadly, including the labor of doing R&D and figuring out how to deploy the technology itself, you're changing the input that generated the steady trend in the first place. If you zoom out further than 150 years, growth has actually accelerated a great deal over the long run. Going from hunter-gatherer to agricultural to industrial growth rates involved big jumps. So there's a competing outside view that says the two-percent era is the anomaly, and a technology that lets you scale up the number of "minds" working on the economy could plausibly put us on a new growth regime.

I don't think the bottleneck arguments are wrong. I think they're the most serious part of the skeptical case, and they could mean the transition takes years rather than months. But I'd want people to ask which bottlenecks are truly fundamental and which ones exist mainly because humans are slow and scarce. A lot of the friction we see today is the friction of coordinating human labor, and that's exactly the thing that might change.

r001.rationale: The response says that over roughly 150 years, major technologies transformed daily life but produced no large spikes in aggregate growth, which stayed near 2% per capita.

r002.rationale: It describes the view that important technologies are absorbed into the economy at a pace that keeps growth near its roughly 2% trend despite continued innovation.

r003.rationale: It grounds expectations of slow AI-driven change in decades-long diffusion, bottlenecks, and institutional and social friction, and says these could stretch the transition to years rather than months.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the strongest version of the outside view goes something like this. Historically, transformative technologies have taken a long time to actually show up in the productivity statistics. Electricity is the classic example. You have the dynamo in the 1880s, and it's not until the 1920s that you see a big productivity boost in American manufacturing, because factories had to be completely redesigned around the new technology rather than just swapping a steam engine for an electric motor. Computers are another one. Solow's famous quip in 1987 was that you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. And then it took another decade or so before that showed up.

So the argument is that even if the underlying technology is quite powerful, there are all these frictions. Firms have to figure out how to reorganize their workflows. There's regulation, there's liability, there's the fact that most of the economy is made up of fairly conservative institutions that don't adopt things quickly. There are complementary investments that have to happen. And on top of that, a lot of the economy is in sectors like healthcare, education, construction, government, where productivity growth has been very slow for decades regardless of what technology was available. Baumol's cost disease and all that. So the expectation is that AI diffuses the way previous general purpose technologies diffused, which is gradually, and you get maybe a bump in growth rates of a percentage point or two rather than something that looks like a discontinuity.

And I think the people who hold this view also point to the track record of forecasters who predicted rapid change and were wrong. There's a long history of people saying automation is going to eliminate most jobs within a decade, going back to the fifties and sixties, and that didn't happen. So there's a reasonable prior that says, when someone tells you this time is different, you should discount that pretty heavily.

I take that seriously. Where I end up disagreeing is mostly on whether AI is actually in the reference class of previous general purpose technologies. The thing that makes AI different, if the technology gets to where I think it could get, is that it's not a tool that makes human workers more productive, it's a substitute for the workers themselves, including the workers who do the adopting and the reorganizing and the complementary innovation. So the bottleneck in the electricity case was that you needed humans to figure out how to redesign the factory. If the AI can do that part too, a lot of the frictions that drove slow diffusion historically could get compressed. But I want to be clear that's a claim about the technology reaching a certain level of capability, and if it stalls out at something more like a very good autocomplete, then I think the outside view is probably right and you should expect something that looks a lot more like the computer revolution.

r001.rationale: It says past technologies took time to appear in productivity statistics, but does not state that they failed to raise frontier economies’ roughly 2% growth rate.

r002.rationale: It describes gradual AI diffusion and modest growth gains, but does not explain that ongoing innovation prevents economic growth from slowing.

r003.rationale: It cites adoption frictions and past overpredictions of rapid change as reasons to expect AI’s economic effects to arrive gradually.

astra-6.text:
I think the outside view is something like: historically, even very important technologies have taken a long time to show up as big changes in economic growth. You can have an impressive demonstration, or even a product that’s useful to a lot of people, without immediately transforming the economy. Firms have to reorganize, people have to figure out how to use the technology, and complementary investments have to happen. So you should be skeptical of a story where we see exciting AI capabilities and then, a couple of years later, everything is different.

And I think that’s a reasonable starting point. The question is how much AI resembles those previous technologies. If you think of it as another tool that makes workers more productive at particular tasks, then gradual diffusion makes a lot of sense. If you think it could eventually substitute for human labor across a very broad range of tasks, including doing research and developing the next generation of AI, then there’s a potential feedback loop that the historical analogy doesn’t necessarily capture.

So I’d distinguish between ‘it takes time to integrate a new tool into the economy’ and ‘the economy will change slowly even once you can automate most cognitive work.’ The historical evidence seems much more directly relevant to the first claim than the second.

r001.rationale: The response says major technologies can take a long time to affect growth, but does not state that advances over the past 100–150 years failed to raise frontier economies’ roughly 2% growth rate.

r002.rationale: It mentions gradual diffusion and integration costs, but does not explain the view that ongoing technological innovation prevents economic growth from slowing.

r003.rationale: It presents the outside view that important technologies take time to transform the economy, citing organizational change and complementary investments, and urges skepticism about rapid change after exciting AI capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the outside view is basically that we’ve had a lot of really important technologies before, and even when they’re transformative, it takes a long time for that transformation to show up in the economy. You have to reorganize firms, build complementary infrastructure, figure out how to use the technology effectively. So if you think of AI as another technology in that sequence, you might expect substantial productivity gains, but spread out over decades.

And I think that’s a reasonable starting point. The question is how much weight to put on it if AI can eventually substitute for human cognitive labor very broadly, including the work of doing research and developing better AI. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop that isn’t captured very well by the analogy to adopting a new tool. So I understand the slow-change view as a strong historical prior, but I’m less convinced that the historical analogy continues to apply as AI starts automating the process of technological progress itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transformative technologies taking time to affect the economy, but does not state that major advances over the past 100–150 years failed to raise frontier economies’ roughly 2% growth rate.

r002.rationale: It says productivity gains may arrive over decades; it does not explain that continued technological innovation is viewed as preventing economic growth from slowing.

r003.rationale: The response describes adoption delays and needed adjustments, but does not identify a general expectation that change is harder and slower than people anticipate.
